paper_title: LiveVAE: Causal Window Attention Makes Efficient Streaming Video VAE

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: While video diffusion models have grown faster and increasingly streamable, the video VAE remains a primary latency bottleneck across interactive generation and editing pipelines. Existing VAEs and their acceleration methods rely mainly on heavy convolutions or full frame attention, and most focus only on decoding, leaving encoding costly for streaming conditional generation and editing. This raises a natural question: Do video VAE encoding and decoding actually require such global spatiotemporal modeling? By analyzing the effective receptive fields of pretrained video VAEs, we find that both encoding and decoding a patch rely almost entirely on its spatial and temporal neighbors. To exploit this strong locality, we introduce LiveVAE, a streaming encoder and decoder built on causal window attention, which cuts per frame compute while keeping the temporal KV cache bounded for streaming. Decoupled encoder/decoder distillation followed by joint finetuning preserves the pretrained latent space, making LiveVAE a drop-in replacement for the original VAE. On MiniMax-H3, LiveVAE achieves 5.2-6.2x faster encoding and 3.0-3.3x faster decoding than the official VAE with higher PSNR. Paired with our dedicated inference infrastructure, LiveVAE pushes the speedup to 13.4x with almost no quality loss. Code and models will be released.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Video diffusion models (Rombach et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2025; Wan Team, 2025; Kong et al., 2024) increasingly target real time generation, streaming video editing, and reference to video generation. Such models comprise two core components: video VAE (Kingma & Welling, 2014) that maps between pixels and compact latent space, and diffusion Transformer (Peebles & Xie, 2023) that generates within this latent space. Recent advances in causal diffusion with KV caching (Chen et al., 2024; Yin et al., 2025) and few step autoregressive distillation (Huang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026) have reduced DiT sampling to just few causal steps, shifting the primary latency bottleneck to the video VAE. In real time generation, the Wan2.2 VAE decoder alone accounts for 64.6% of total inference time at 720p (Shin et al., 2026; Kang & Kwak, 2026). Moreover, in streaming video editing and reference to video generation, the encoder must compress incoming video frames or visual references into latents on the fly, step that can take even longer than decoding (Zhao et al., 2026). Supporting these interactive pipelines therefore requires fast streaming for both encoding and decoding, rather than decoding alone. Existing video VAEs and acceleration methods struggle to meet these requirements. Mainstream video VAEs rely on heavy causal 3D convolutions (Yu et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025; Wan Team, 2025; Kong et al., 2024) whose computational cost scales rapidly with resolution, and prior acceleration efforts focus almost exclusively on the decoder while leaving streaming encoding largely unexplored. Among decoder only methods, distilling or pruning convolutional architectures (Boer Bohan, 2025; Gu et al., 2026; Zou et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026) often trades reconstruction fidelity for speed or retains substantial convolutional overhead. Streaming Transformer decoders, e.g. FlashDecoder (Kang & Kwak, 2026), bound temporal history with KV cache but still attend over the entire latent, incurring quadratic cost in the number of spatial tokens. This raises fundamental question: Do video VAE encoding and decoding actually require such global spatiotemporal modeling? 1 Figure 1: Speed and Quality on MiniMax-H3. Top: LiveVAE compared with other methods in PSNR and decoding and encoding FPS at 720p. Reconstruction Quality: zoomed crops of the yellow box from each VAE. Generation Quality: Reference to video results on CodeVideoBench (Liang et al., 2026) with the H3 VAE and ours. Figure 2: Effective Receptive Field analysis of Pretrained VAEs. To answer this question, we analyze the effective receptive fields (Luo et al., 2016) of pretrained video VAEs, including MiniMax-H3 (MiniMax, 2026) and Wan2.2 (Wan Team, 2025), using normalized squared input gradients, and cross check the temporal behavior with gradient free frame replacement test (Zeiler & Fergus, 2014; Huang et al., 2018). As shown in Fig. 2, the dependencies between input and output concentrate around the target in both encoders and decoders. Spatially, compact 7 7 neighborhood around the target location holds 95100% of the gradient energy in Fig. 2b. Temporally, 2 the current and immediately preceding steps hold 7199% in Fig. 2c. Replacing single input step changes the output two steps later by only 0.51.5% for the decoders and 412% for the encoders, relative to the change caused by replacing the entire sequence. To exploit this locality, we introduce LiveVAE, streaming video encoder and decoder built on causal window attention. Spatially, restricting attention to local window eliminates redundant computation to lower latency and enables direct extrapolation to higher resolutions by modeling only local patterns. Temporally, the causal window bounds the KV cache for continuous streaming. To preserve the pretrained latent space, we train LiveVAE via three stage distillation framework. We first independently distill the encoder and decoder in latent and pixel spaces against the frozen pretrained VAE, and then jointly finetune both modules end to end. This alignment allows LiveVAE to directly replace the original VAE. On MiniMax-H3 (MiniMax, 2026), LiveVAE achieves 5.26.2 faster encoding and 3.03.3 faster decoding than the official VAE while matching or exceeding its PSNR from 480p to 2160p. To further translate this architectural efficiency into hardware speedups, we build dedicated inference infrastructure (Section 3.4) incorporating attention operator fusion, region wise compilation, and FP8 quantization aware training. With it, LiveVAE pushes the end to end speedup up to 13.4 with negligible quality loss, matching the official VAE in downstream reference to video generation. In summary, our contributions are as follows: Through effective receptive field and perturbation analyses of pretrained video VAEs, we show that video encoding and decoding rely almost entirely on local spatial and temporal neighborhoods. We propose LiveVAE, the first Transformer based streaming video encoder and decoder built on causal window attention, which eliminates redundant computation to lower latency, extrapolates from 720p to 2160p with even higher PSNR, and bounds the temporal KV cache. We design three stage distillation framework that preserves the pretrained latent space, enabling LiveVAE to directly replace the original VAE. We develop dedicated inference infrastructure for LiveVAE, pushing end to end speedup up to 13.4 on MiniMax-H3 with almost no quality loss.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Latent Diffusion Models. Latent diffusion (Rombach et al., 2022) trains the generator in the compact latent space of pretrained VAE (Kingma & Welling, 2014), and diffusion Transformers (DiTs) (Peebles & Xie, 2023) have scaled this recipe to video (Yang et al., 2025; Wan Team, 2025; Kong et al., 2024; HaCohen et al., 2024; NVIDIA, 2025). The latent space is the representation the DiT learns from, and the quality of this representation largely determines how fast the DiT converges and how well it generates (Yu et al., 2025; Singh et al., 2026; Yao et al., 2025). Existing work therefore designs the latent space for the generator. One line raises the compression ratio so that the DiT processes fewer tokens (Chen et al., 2025; HaCohen et al., 2024), with causal 3D convolutions that compress time as well (Yu et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025). Another aligns the latents with pretrained visual representations. VA-VAE (Yao et al., 2025) aligns them with vision foundation models to ease the tradeoff between reconstruction and generation, and REPA-E (Leng et al., 2025) tunes the VAE and the DiT end to end through such an alignment. third uses these representations directly as latents. RAE (Zheng et al., 2026) pairs frozen representation encoder with trained decoder. Each design defines new latent space on which the DiT is then trained, and once the DiT is trained, this latent space is fixed. CV-VAE (Zhao et al., 2024) thus keeps new video VAE compatible with the latent space of pretrained image VAE. Our work is orthogonal to these designs. Whichever latent space DiT is trained on, we keep it and replace only the encoder and decoder that compute it with streaming ones. Streaming Video Generation. On the generator side, video generation has become causal and fast. Diffusion Forcing (Chen et al., 2024) and CausVid (Yin et al., 2025) generate one frame at time with KV cache, and Self Forcing (Huang et al., 2025) and Rolling Forcing (Liu et al., 2026) close the train-test gap and generate long videos in real time with few denoising steps. Once the generator needs only few causal steps, the bottleneck shifts to the VAE. Few step autoregressive distillation raises the decoders share of latency by more than ten times (Zhu et al., 2026), the Wan2.2 decoder takes 64.6% of the inference time of MotionStream (Shin et al., 2026) at 720p (Kang & Kwak, 2026), and in streaming video editing, where the input video is also encoded, VAE encoding takes longer than decoding (Zhao et al., 2026). Streaming generation thus needs both streaming decoder and streaming encoder. Video VAE Acceleration. Almost all video VAE acceleration methods accelerate only the decoder. We group them by whether they keep the latent space of the DiT. Lightweight VAEs trained from scratch (Cheng et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025) define new latent space, so the DiT must be retrained or finetuned. The others keep the latent space. Distilled and pruned decoders reduce per frame cost. TAEHV (Boer Bohan, 2025) and LightVAE (Gu et al., 2026) distill lighter decoder that trades fidelity for speed, while Turbo-VAED (Zou et al., 2026) and Flash-VAED (Zhu et al., 2026) prune and replace the original decoders causal 3D convolutions, whose cost still grows with resolution. Streaming 3 Figure 3: Overview of LiveVAE. (a) Encoder and Decoder architecture of LiveVAE. (b) Causal Window Attention. (c) Three stage progressive distillation. (d) Streaming Inference with bounded KV cache. decoders instead reduce latency by decoding as the latents arrive. Some make bidirectional decoder causal (Chen et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026), and FlashDecoder (Kang & Kwak, 2026), closest to ours, is Transformer decoder that streams one latent frame at time with rolling KV cache. Its tokens attend to the full current and previous frames, so its cost grows quadratically with resolution, and it requires multiresolution training up to higher resolution; ours attend to fixed local window, scale linearly, and are trained only at low resolutions, yet extrapolate directly to higher resolutions at inference time.

sections.title: 3.4 Inference Infrastructure Optimization
sections.content: To further accelerate streaming inference, we introduce three system optimizations on NVIDIA H100 GPUs rented from RunPod that yield up to 3.0 end to end speedup with negligible quality loss  (Fig. 5)  . These optimizations are enabled only for Ours-Opt in Table 1. Attention Operator Fusion. Running query key normalization, 3D RoPE, 2D window attention, and the cross frame merge of Eq. (5) separately incurs heavy memory traffic from intermediate tensors. We fuse query key normalization with 3D RoPE into one kernel and fold the cross frame merge directly into the window attention kernel, so that the fused attention path reads and writes global memory only at its inputs and outputs. The window attention kernel attends over the full causal window with an online softmax, so the merge needs no separate pass. Region Wise Compilation. Compiling the whole model with torch.compile suffers from graph breaks around custom attention kernels and recompilations during KV cache warmup. Instead, we compile only the four static subgraphs in each block, namely the normalization before attention, QKV projection, output projection, and the residual FFN, while leaving the CWA kernels and cache control flow uncompiled in the outer loop. FFN FP8 with QAT. With attention made lightweight, the FFN dominates computation, so we quantize the FFN linear layers to FP8 in all encoder blocks and in every decoder block except the last. To avoid the quality drop of direct posttraining quantization, we apply quantization aware training, denoted QAT, under Eq. (12) by simulating FP8 precision during finetuning. Attention and normalization retain their original precision. Choice of layers. We enable FP8 in one block at time on the model before QAT and measure the change in reconstruction PSNR. The cost is concentrated in the last block of each network: at 480p, PSNR drops by about 0.9 dB for the last encoder block and by more than 7 dB for the last decoder block, against about 0.1 dB for the other 22 blocks together. The inputs of the last decoder FFN far exceed the range of FP8, so part of them saturates. This loss appears to come from dynamic range rather than from rounding precision, which we expect finetuning to recover less easily, while leaving one block out costs little speed. We therefore quantize the FFN of all 12 encoder blocks and of the first 11 decoder blocks, and keep the last decoder block in its original precision. The last encoder block stays quantized, and its loss is the main part that QAT has to recover. QAT training. QAT starts from the model after Stage 3 and continues training with the quantized forward pass, so that the weights adapt to the deterministic error of FP8. It rests on the following four choices. Deployed forward pass, straight through gradients. The forward pass simulates FP8 by calling the same FP8 multiplication as the inference engine, so training and deployment see the same values. For quantized linear layer with input and weight Θ, = FP8(a, Θ) + (cid:0)aΘ sg[aΘ](cid:1) (15) where FP8(a, Θ) is the deployed FP8 product. The bracket is zero in the forward pass, so takes the FP8 value, while the gradients are those of the ordinary linear layer, as in straight through estimator. Floating point weights. Only the quantized layers are updated, and the optimizer always updates their floating point weights. The quantized forward pass adds no parameter and no running statistic, so the checkpoint keeps the format of the unquantized model and is converted to FP8 only once, at deployment time. Unchanged objective. The objective, the loss weights and the data mix follow Stage 3, so that the change is limited to FP8. The latent alignment terms keep the encoder in the latent space of the teacher while its weights adapt to the quantization error of FP8. Delayed adversarial term. sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Base VAEs and models. To demonstrate the generalizability of our method across distinct latent representations, we distill LiveVAE from two pretrained video VAEs, MiniMax-H3 (MiniMax, 2026), denoted H3, and Wan2.2 (Wan Team, 2025). We call each of them base VAE and its encoder and decoder the official encoder and decoder; they are the teachers of Section 3.3. All student encoders and decoders use 12 Transformer layers and causal attention window of size 2 7 7. The hidden dimensions of the encoder and the decoder are 2048 and 2560 for H3, and 2560 and 2496 for Wan2.2. Training data. We train on an internal collection of videos and images, filtered for motion intensity and category diversity, with images making up 20% of the training samples in all three stages. Videos are 46 clips sampled at 8 to 30 FPS, from which we take 22 frames for H3 and 21 for Wan2.2, at resolution of 480p or 720p. Training details. All stages use global batch size of 8 and AdamW with β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.95, weight decay of 0.01 and learning rate of 104, with 1k warmup steps and cosine decay to zero. Stages 1, 2 and 3 take 80k, 200k and 5k steps, and Stage 3 keeps an EMA of the weights with decay of 0.999. In all stages, the ℓ1 and LPIPS terms of Eq. (8) have weights of 1 and λp = 0.33; the others are λz = 1.0, λKL = 103 and λadv = 0.1. Baselines. We compare with TAEHV (Boer Bohan, 2025), LightTAE (LightX2V Team, 2025), LightVAE (Gu et al., 2026), Turbo-VAED (Zou et al., 2026), LynnReal-Omni (Mao et al., 2026), Solar-X (Chen et al., 2026) and StreamRenderH3 (Lu et al., 2026), using their public weights for the two base VAEs. We run all of them ourselves and evaluate every row of Table 1 by end to end reconstruction. decoder only baseline is paired with the official encoder of its base VAE; for ours, we also report the two combinations that replace single official component (Section 4.2.5). sections.title: 4.2 Main Results
sections.content: 4.2.1 Reconstruction Quality In Table 1, LiveVAE exceeds the official H3 teacher in PSNR at all four resolutions by 0.070.90 dB, the highest among all methods from 720p upward. Its LPIPS gap to the official H3 VAE narrows from .054 versus .041 at 480p to .034 versus .029 at 2160p and stays close to the streaming decoder only baselines. On both Wan2.2 and H3, Ours outperforms every baseline that replaces both the encoder and the decoder on all metrics, by 3.010.5 dB in PSNR. LightVAE-Pro and Turbo-VAED on Wan2.2 and LynnReal-Omni on H3 reach comparable or slightly higher quality at some resolutions, but they replace only the decoder and keep the official encoder at its original speed. 4.2.2 Inference Efficiency Tiny models such as TAEH3, TAEW2.2 and LightTAE are faster but trail Ours by more than 4 dB in PSNR. On H3, where official encoding is slower than decoding, Ours accelerates the encoder by 5.26.2 and the decoder by 3.03.3, whereas the decoder only LynnReal-Omni, Solar-X and StreamRender-H3 reach only 1.31.7 on the decoder and keep the official encoder. With the inference optimizations of Section 3.4, Ours-Opt reaches up to 18.7 and 9.5 within 0.13 dB PSNR. Ours also halves H3 peak memory at 480p from 8.8 to 4.4 GB and needs only 14.1 GB at 2160p, where Solar-X runs out of memory and StreamRender-H3 uses 53.2 GB. On Wan2.2, Ours speeds up decoding by 4.76.5 against 1.61.8 for LightVAE-Pro and Turbo-VAED, speeds up encoding by 1.41.6, and cuts peak memory at 2160p from 55.9 to 15.7 GB, where LightVAE-Pro and Turbo-VAED need 54 GB or more. 4.2.3 Generation Quality Text to video generation. We evaluate text to video generation on VBench-2.0 (Zheng et al., 2025) in Table 2 with frozen few step DiTs: the 3 step FastWan2.2-TI2V-5B (Zhang et al., 2025) for Wan2.2 and the 4 step Wuli MiniMax-H3 Turbo LoRA (Wuli-art, 2026) for H3. Replacing the decoder on Wan2.2 preserves the overall score at 0.581 versus 0.582, with slight gains in Human Fidelity and Physics. On MiniMax-H3, Ours stays within 0.01 of the official decoder on Creativity, Controllability, and Commonsense, with minor drops in Human Fidelity at 0.784 versus 0.830 and Physics at 0.781 versus 0.802. Reference to video generation. Following CodeVideoBench (Liang et al., 2026) with the official MiniMax-H3 weights (MiniMax, 2026), replacing both the H3 encoder and decoder in Table 2 yields nearly identical total of 84.0 versus 84.1, improving Style from 86.7 to 87.7 while preserving Structure and Quality, which confirms that both modules remain well aligned with the frozen DiT latent space.

sections.title: 4.2.4 Resolution Extrapolation
sections.content: Trained only at 480p and 720p, LiveVAE extrapolates directly to 1080p and 2160p without finetuning and outperforms the H3 teacher (MiniMax, 2026) in PSNR, aided by local spatial windows and DiT aligned 3D RoPE. Because causal window attention scales linearly with token count, scaling from 720p to 2160p increases H3 encoding and decoding latencies by only 7.9 and 8.1.

sections.title: 4.3.3 Ablation on Inference Infrastructure
sections.content: Fig. 5 adds the optimizations of Section 3.4 to our full model: is attention operator fusion, region wise compilation, and FFN FP8 with QAT. Ours already uses the frame wise 2D decomposition. Table 12 in Appendix gives the time, memory and quality of each cumulative step at all four resolutions. Optimized runtime. Fig. 5(a) reports the end to end speedup, i.e. the encoding plus decoding time of Ours for 22 frame clip divided by that of each runtime. Attention operator fusion gives 1.71.8 at every resolution by removing the intermediate tensors between normalization, RoPE, window attention and the cross frame merge, and region wise compilation raises it to 2.5 at 720p and 1080p and 2.2 at 2160p. FP8 helps only at high resolution: it raises the speedup to 3.0 at 1080p and 2.7 at 2160p but lowers it to 2.1 at 720p and 1.0 at 480p, because its fixed overhead outweighs the saving at low token counts. FP8 also raises the end to end peak memory by 1.4 to 1.7 GB, so we recommend enabling FP8 only at resolutions of 1080p and above. QAT. Fig. 5(b) reports the PSNR change relative to Ours. FP8 applied directly to the trained model lowers PSNR by 1.35 dB at 480p and 3.43 dB at 2160p. QAT recovers it to within 0.13 dB of Ours at every resolution, e.g. 39.07 dB against 39.05 dB at 2160p. QAT training is described in Section 3.4.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented LiveVAE, streaming video VAE that accelerates both encoding and decoding while preserving pretrained latent space. Our key finding is that small spatial neighborhood and short causal temporal window suffice for both components. Causal window attention enables streaming with bounded KV cache, while three stage distillation maintains compatibility with existing DiTs without retraining. Attention operator fusion, region wise compilation and FFN FP8 with QAT further reduce inference latency. On MiniMax-H3, LiveVAE encodes 5.26.2 and decodes 3.03.3 faster than the official VAE at matching or higher PSNR, and generalizes from training at 720p and below to inference at up to 2160p. Limitations and future work. Despite these gains, LiveVAE retains perceptual quality gap. Fine details can become blurred  (Fig. 6)  , and VBench-2.0 Human Fidelity and Physics remain below the official decoder on MiniMax-H3. We attribute part of this gap to latent space that was learned by convolutional VAE. Improving perceptual reconstruction and generation quality without increasing streaming latency is direction for future work. Figure 6: Failure cases.
